claim: R-loops are three-stranded structures that form when transcripts hybridize to chromosomal DNA.
source: R-loops, three-stranded structures that form when transcripts hybridize to chromosomal DNA, are potent agents of genome instability.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about R-loop structure.

claim: R-loops are potent agents of genome instability.
source: R-loops, three-stranded structures that form when transcripts hybridize to chromosomal DNA, are potent agents of genome instability.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Depleting endogenous RNase H activity impairs R-loop removal in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Depleting endogenous RNase H activity impairs R-loop removal in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, causing DNA damage that occurs preferentially in the repetitive ribosomal DNA locus (rDNA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing R-loop accumulation in RNase H mutants, as shown in Figure 1D and referenced in the text.

claim: Depleting endogenous RNase H activity causes DNA damage that occurs preferentially in the repetitive ribosomal DNA locus (rDNA).
source: Depleting endogenous RNase H activity impairs R-loop removal in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, causing DNA damage that occurs preferentially in the repetitive ribosomal DNA locus (rDNA).
evidence: This is supported by data showing Rad52-GFP foci co-localization with the nucleolus and citations to previous work.

claim: The persistence of R-loops at sites of DNA damage induces repair by break-induced replication (BIR).
source: We present a model that the persistence of R-loops at sites of DNA damage induces repair by break-induced replication (BIR).
evidence: This is a model presented based on experimental data showing that BIR inhibition suppresses lethality in RNase H mutants.

claim: R-loop induced BIR is particularly susceptible to the formation of lethal repair intermediates at the rDNA because of a barrier imposed by RNA polymerase I.
source: This R-loop induced BIR is particularly susceptible to the formation of lethal repair intermediates at the rDNA because of a barrier imposed by RNA polymerase I.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that mutations in RNA polymerase I subunit Rpa190 suppress lethality.

claim: RNase H1 and H2 are highly conserved ribonucleases with the ability to degrade the RNA moiety of a DNA:RNA hybrid.
source: RNase H1 and H2 are highly conserved ribonucleases with the ability to degrade the RNA moiety of a DNA:RNA hybrid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNase H enzymes, supported by citation to Cerritelli and Crouch, 2009.

claim: Disrupting the activity of RNase H1 and H2 (rnh1∆ rnh201∆ in Saccharomyces cerevisiae) increases the persistence of DNA:RNA hybrids.
source: Disrupting the activity of the two enzymes (rnh1∆ rnh201∆ in Saccharomyces cerevisiae) has been a useful tool for increasing the persistence of DNA:RNA hybrids and studying the effects of hybrid-induced instability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: In the absence of RNase H activity, the levels of hybrids formed at susceptible loci increase dramatically.
source: Indeed, efforts to map R-loops genome-wide have shown that in the absence of RNase H activity, the levels of hybrids formed at susceptible loci increase dramatically (Wahba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wahba et al., 2016.

claim: The increase in hybrids in RNase H mutants is associated with increased rates of genome instability that include loss of heterozygosity (LOH) events, loss of entire chromosomes, and recombination at the ribosomal locus.
source: This increase in hybrids is associated with increased rates of genome instability that include loss of heterozygosity (LOH) events, loss of entire chromosomes, and recombination at the ribosomal locus (Wahba et al., 2011; O'Connell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wahba et al., 2011 and O'Connell et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 60% of all transcription in S. cerevisiae is devoted to producing ribosomal RNA from about 150 repeated units located in a clustered region on chromosome XII.
source: Approximately 60% of all transcription in S. cerevisiae is devoted to producing ribosomal RNA from about 150 repeated units located in a clustered region on chromosome XII (Warner, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Warner, 1999.

claim: The ribosomal DNA repeats at 9.1 kb each make up about 10% of the budding yeast genome.
source: These repeats, at 9.1 kb each, make up about 10% of the budding yeast genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast genome organization, supported by citation context.

claim: Almost 50% of all R-loops map to the rDNA.
source: Accordingly, almost 50% of all R-loops map to the rDNA (Wahba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wahba et al., 2016.

claim: R-loops found at the rDNA are associated with increased rates of recombination.
source: R-loops found at the rDNA are associated with increased rates of recombination (Wahba et al., 2011, 2013), RNA polymerase pileups (El Hage et al., 2010), and stalled replication forks (Stuckey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wahba et al., 2011, 2013.

claim: R-loops found at the rDNA are associated with RNA polymerase pileups.
source: R-loops found at the rDNA are associated with increased rates of recombination (Wahba et al., 2011, 2013), RNA polymerase pileups (El Hage et al., 2010), and stalled replication forks (Stuckey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to El Hage et al., 2010.

claim: R-loops found at the rDNA are associated with stalled replication forks.
source: R-loops found at the rDNA are associated with increased rates of recombination (Wahba et al., 2011, 2013), RNA polymerase pileups (El Hage et al., 2010), and stalled replication forks (Stuckey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stuckey et al., 2015.

claim: Rad52 is required in almost all homologous recombination (HR) pathways.
source: Rad52 is required in almost all homologous recombination (HR) pathways, and in yeast forms bright foci upon induction of DNA damage (Lisby et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lisby et al., 2001.

claim: Rad52 forms bright foci upon induction of DNA damage in yeast.
source: Rad52 is required in almost all homologous recombination (HR) pathways, and in yeast forms bright foci upon induction of DNA damage (Lisby et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lisby et al., 2001.

claim: Most Rad52-GFP foci appear in the S/G2-M phases of the cell cycle.
source: Most foci appear in the S/G2-M phases of the cell cycle and have a moderate rate of repair – almost all spontaneous Rad52-GFP foci are resolved within 40 min (Lisby et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lisby et al., 2003.

claim: Almost all spontaneous Rad52-GFP foci are resolved within 40 min.
source: Most foci appear in the S/G2-M phases of the cell cycle and have a moderate rate of repair – almost all spontaneous Rad52-GFP foci are resolved within 40 min (Lisby et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lisby et al., 2003.

claim: rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutants display an increase in Rad52-GFP foci.
source: Consistent with phenotypes of increased genomic instability, rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutants display an increase in Rad52-GFP foci.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 27% of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells had Rad52-GFP foci, a ten-fold increase over wild-type, rnh1∆, and rnh201∆ cells.
source: Using Rad52-GFP foci as a marker for DNA damage, we observed that 27% of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells had foci, a ten-fold increase over wild-type, rnh1∆, and rnh201∆ cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The growth of the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ double mutant, but not either of the single mutants, was dramatically impaired by the deletion of RAD52.
source: Consistent with the notion that persistent DNA damage uniquely affects the double mutants, the growth of the double mutant, but not either of the single mutants, was dramatically impaired by the deletion of RAD52 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells lacking RNase H1 and H2 had a larger fraction of persistent R-loop induced damage than wild-type cells or cells lacking only one of the RNases H.
source: Thus, by measures of Rad52-GFP foci and Rad52-dependent growth, cells lacking RNase H1 and H2 had a larger fraction of persistent R-loop induced damage than wild-type cells or cells lacking only one of the RNases H.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The fraction of cells with Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells remained around 10 to 15 percent through S-phase.
source: The fraction of cells with Rad52-GFP foci remained around 10 to 15 percent through S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Additional Rad52-GFP foci appeared at the S/G2-M boundary in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells and accumulated to around 50 percent.
source: Additional foci appeared at the S/G2-M boundary and accumulated to around 50 percent, as reported previously.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citations to previous work.

claim: Around 95% of all nuclei in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells stain positive for R-loops.
source: The increase in foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells did not appear to be due to a cell-cycle dependent increase in hybrid formation, as cytological staining revealed similar levels of R-loops in cells staged in G1, S, and M, with around 95% of all nuclei staining for presence of R-loops (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fraction of cycling cells in G2-M was two-fold higher in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells than wild-type or either RNase H single mutant.
source: We found that the fraction of cycling cells in G2-M, defined as a large-budded morphology with an undivided nucleus, was two-fold higher in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells than wild-type or either RNase H single mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The G2-M cell cycle delay in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells was reduced by deletion of RAD9.
source: This fraction was reduced by deletion of RAD9 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of RAD9 did not decrease the level of Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells.
source: Deletion of RAD9 did not decrease the level of Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells, indicating that focus formation was not dependent on the checkpoint (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Throughout the time-course, the vast majority of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells that retained Rad52-GFP foci were arrested pre-anaphase.
source: Throughout the time-course, the vast majority of cells that retained foci were arrested pre-anaphase, indicating that most cells delayed progression into anaphase until the damage was repaired (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After 330 min, 77 percent of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells with Rad52-GFP foci remained arrested in G2-M before anaphase.
source: For example, after 330 min, the bulk of cells had reached G1 (Figure 2C) and the fraction of cells with Rad52-GFP foci had dropped to 20 percent. Of the cells that retained foci, 77 percent remained arrested in G2-M before anaphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Top1 is thought to clear or prevent R-loops and stalled RNA polymerase I (RNA pol I) complexes at the ribosomal locus by resolving supercoiling.
source: Top1 is thought to clear or prevent R-loops and stalled RNA polymerase I (RNA pol I) complexes at the ribosomal locus by resolving supercoiling (El Hage et al., 2010; Drolet et al., 1995; Massé and Drolet, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to El Hage et al., 2010; Drolet et al., 1995; Massé and Drolet, 1999.

claim: Cells with either the top1∆ mutation or the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutations are viable, but the top1∆ rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutant is inviable.
source: A potential synergistic relationship between Top1 and the RNases H came from the observation that while cells with either the top1∆ mutation or the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutations are viable, the top1∆ rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutant is inviable (El Hage et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to El Hage et al., 2010 and experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells with the Top1 inhibitor camptothecin led to increased Rad52-GFP foci that co-localized with the nucleolus.
source: Furthermore, treatment of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells with the Top1 inhibitor camptothecin led to increased Rad52-GFP foci that co-localized with the nucleolus (Stuckey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stuckey et al., 2015.

claim: rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells failed to grow when treated with auxin.
source: Consistent with published results, rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells failed to grow when treated with auxin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TOP1-AID, rnh1∆ TOP1-AID, and rnh201∆ TOP1-AID mutants grew well when treated with auxin.
source: In contrast, TOP1-AID, rnh1∆ TOP1-AID, and rnh201∆ TOP1-AID mutants grew well.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The synergistic lethality occurred only when both RNases H and Top1 were inactivated.
source: Thus, the synergistic lethality occurred only when both RNases H and Top1 were inactivated.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from Figure 3A.

claim: Rad52-GFP foci nearly doubled in the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells compared to an untreated control when treated with auxin for four hours.
source: However, foci nearly doubled in the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells compared to an untreated control, such that a large majority of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells (85%) had foci.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After four hours of treatment with auxin, over 98 percent of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells were arrested pre-anaphase at the G2-M checkpoint.
source: Furthermore, after four hours of treatment with auxin, over 98 percent of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells were arrested pre-anaphase at the G2-M checkpoint (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The cell-cycle arrest of the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID was Rad9 dependent.
source: As with rnh1Δ rnh201Δ cells, the cell-cycle arrest of the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID was Rad9 dependent – deletion of RAD9 resulted in cells that proceeded into the following G1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deletion of RAD9 did not restore viability to rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells treated with auxin.
source: Importantly, deletion of RAD9 did not restore viability to rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells treated with auxin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The inviability of the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ triple mutant was not simply due to the constitutive activation of the checkpoint but rather to the presence of irreparable damage.
source: This result suggested that the inviability of the triple mutant was not simply due to the constitutive activation of the checkpoint but rather to the presence of irreparable damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that RAD9 deletion does not restore viability.

claim: Top1 activity was required after the completion of bulk S-phase to prevent focus formation in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells.
source: This result suggested that Top1 activity was required after the completion of bulk S-phase to prevent focus formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The fraction of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells that survived transient auxin treatment was around 16 percent, similar to the percentage of cells that did not have Rad52 foci when given the same treatment.
source: The fraction of cells that survived, relative to an untreated control, was around 16 percent, similar to the percentage of cells that did not have Rad52 foci when given the same treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transiently depleting Top1 in S-phase in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells did not lead to loss of viability.
source: Transiently depleting Top1 in S-phase, in which Rad52-GFP foci levels remain unchanged (18%), did not lead to loss of viability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transiently depleting Top1 in mid-M phase in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells led to elevated foci levels (75%) and a dramatic increase in lethality.
source: However, transiently depleting Top1 in mid-M phase, which led to elevated foci levels (75%), also led to a dramatic increase in lethality.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of Top1 activity in G2-M in cells lacking the RNases H led to irreparable DNA damage in the vast majority of cells.
source: These results suggested that depletion of Top1 activity in G2-M in cells lacking the RNases H led to irreparable DNA damage in the vast majority of cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from Figure 4C.

claim: PIF1-E467G suppressed auxin sensitivity when introduced into rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells.
source: This allele suppressed auxin sensitivity when introduced into rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells, indicating its responsibility for the suppression of lethality in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both pif1∆ and pif1-m2 were able to suppress the auxin sensitivity of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells.
source: When introduced into rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID, both pif1∆ and pif1-m2, an allele that maintains mitochondrial but not nuclear functions of Pif1 (Schulz and Zakian, 1994), were able to suppress the auxin sensitivity of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citation to Schulz and Zakian, 1994.

claim: PIF1-E467G likely inactivated a nuclear activity that contributed to hybrid-induced lethality.
source: We concluded that PIF1-E467G likely inactivated a nuclear activity that contributed to hybrid-induced lethality (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that pif1-m2 (which maintains mitochondrial but not nuclear function) also suppresses lethality.

claim: The PIF1-E467G allele did not prevent hybrid induced DNA damage.
source: These results suggested that the PIF1-E467G allele did not prevent hybrid induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C showing similar levels of Rad52-GFP foci accumulation.

claim: Cells with PIF1-E467G gradually resolved most of their Rad52-GFP foci as they completed mitosis.
source: In contrast to rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells, which maintained 85% Rad52-GFP foci and never proceeded through anaphase, cells with PIF1-E467G gradually resolved most of their foci as they completed mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PIF1-E467G promoted the repair of hybrid-induced damage.
source: We therefore concluded that PIF1-E467G promoted the repair of hybrid-induced damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Pif1 helicase contributes to BIR processivity.
source: The Pif1 helicase contributes to this processivity (Davis and Symington, 2004; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davis and Symington, 2004 and Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: In a wild-type strain, the frequency of BIR using the 30 kb template was approximately 12%.
source: In a wild-type strain, the frequency of BIR using the 30 kb template was approximately 12%, consistent with previously published results (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the absence of a functional Pif1 allele (pif1-m2), repair by BIR dropped to approximately 5%.
source: In the absence of a functional Pif1 allele (pif1-m2), repair by BIR dropped to approximately 5%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The frequency of BIR in cells carrying PIF1-E467G dropped to around 3%.
source: Similarly, the frequency of BIR in cells carrying PIF1-E467G dropped to around 3%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PIF1-E467G inhibited BIR.
source: This led us to conclude that PIF1-E467G inhibited BIR.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Deleting POL32 in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells suppressed auxin sensitivity.
source: To test this model further, we deleted POL32 in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells (Figure 5B). Pol32 is a non-essential subunit of the primary BIR polymerase (Polδ), and is required for replication fork processivity (Wilson et al., 2013). These strains were no longer sensitive to auxin, corroborating the conclusion that inhibiting BIR was sufficient to allow for repair of otherwise lethal hybrid-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citation to Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibiting BIR was sufficient to allow for repair of otherwise lethal hybrid-induced DNA damage.
source: These strains were no longer sensitive to auxin, corroborating the conclusion that inhibiting BIR was sufficient to allow for repair of otherwise lethal hybrid-induced DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that POL32 deletion suppresses lethality.

claim: The inability to repair DNA damage in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells depleted of Top1 was caused by BIR processivity.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that the inability to repair DNA damage in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells depleted of Top1 was caused by BIR processivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that inhibiting BIR processivity suppresses lethality.

claim: PIF1-E467G cells had a total level of repair that was 5-fold greater than wild-type cells in the 80 kb repair strain.
source: As expected if this repair was independent of BIR, this alternative pathway was as efficient with the 80 kb repair template as it was in cells with the 30 kb repair template – PIF1-E467G cells in the 80 kb repair strain had a total level of repair that was 5-fold greater than wild-type cells but only six percent of which was repaired using BIR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The increase in repair in PIF1-E467G cells was not due to increased non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
source: The increase in repair was not due to increased non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), as less than one percent of cells of all genotypes retained a telomeric drug resistance marker (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: All strains efficiently induced DSBs, as evidenced by the failure to PCR-amplify DNA surrounding the cut site after HO induction.
source: Additionally, all strains efficiently induced DSBs, as evidenced by the failure to PCR-amplify DNA surrounding the cut site after HO induction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The majority of Rad52-GFP foci seen in RNase H mutants co-localize with the nucleolus.
source: These alleles were particularly intriguing because previous studies have shown that the majority of Rad52-GFP foci seen in RNase H mutants co-localize with the nucleolus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lethal events seen in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells were rDNA-specific.
source: This suggested that the lethal events seen in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells were rDNA-specific (Stuckey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-localization of foci with the nucleolus, supported by citation to Stuckey et al., 2015.

claim: Efficient repair of a DSB on chromosome V by BIR and NHEJ occurred in top1∆ and rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed efficient repair of a DSB on chromosome V by BIR and NHEJ in top1∆ and rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Topological stress and persistent R-loops were particularly problematic in the rDNA.
source: These results suggested that topological stress and persistent R-loops were particularly problematic in the rDNA (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing rDNA-specific lethality.

claim: Both RPA190 alleles suppressed the auxin-induced inviability of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells.
source: RPA190-K1482T and RPA190-V1486F shared the suppression phenotypes of PIF1-E467G. Both RPA190 alleles suppressed the auxin-induced inviability of rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Neither RPA190-K1482T nor RPA190-V1486F prevented the accumulation of high levels of Rad52-GFP foci, but rather allowed for their repair.
source: Similarly, neither allele prevented the accumulation of high levels of foci, but rather allowed for their repair (Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The lethality in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells was due to irreparable hybrid-induced DNA damage in the ribosomal repeats.
source: Given the specificity of RNA pol I for transcribing regions of the rDNA locus, these results strongly suggested that the lethality in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells was due to irreparable hybrid-induced DNA damage in the ribosomal repeats, and that altering the function of RNA polymerase I allowed this damage to be repaired.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of RNA pol I and the suppression by RPA190 mutations.

claim: Altering the function of RNA polymerase I allowed hybrid-induced DNA damage to be repaired.
source: Given the specificity of RNA pol I for transcribing regions of the rDNA locus, these results strongly suggested that the lethality in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells was due to irreparable hybrid-induced DNA damage in the ribosomal repeats, and that altering the function of RNA polymerase I allowed this damage to be repaired.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that RPA190 mutations suppress lethality.

claim: Residues K1482 and V1486 map to the 'jaw' domain of RNA pol I, along potential contacts with the non-essential RNA pol I subunit Rpa12.
source: Residues K1482 and V1486 map to the 'jaw' domain of RNA pol I, along potential contacts with the non-essential RNA pol I subunit Rpa12 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3) (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from citations to Engel et al., 2013 and Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013, and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rpa12 has a role in promoting RNA pol I backtracking and transcript termination.
source: Rpa12 has a role in promoting RNA pol I backtracking and transcript termination (Kuhn et al., 2007; Martinez-Rucobo and Cramer, 1829).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuhn et al., 2007 and Martinez-Rucobo and Cramer, 1829.

claim: Backtracked RNA polymerases can cause R-loop dependent DSBs due to co-directional collisions with replisomes.
source: This backtracking activity may affect genome stability – studies in bacteria have shown that backtracked RNA polymerases can cause R-loop dependent DSBs due to co-directional collisions with replisomes (Dutta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dutta et al., 2011.

claim: Deleting Rpa12 in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ RPA190-K1482T cells was lethal.
source: To test this idea, we knocked out Rpa12 in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ RPA190-K1482T cells (Figure 7B). Deleting Rpa12 in these cells was lethal, indicating that our new RPA190 alleles depended upon Rpa12.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The new RPA190 alleles depended upon Rpa12.
source: Deleting Rpa12 in these cells was lethal, indicating that our new RPA190 alleles depended upon Rpa12.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing lethality when Rpa12 is deleted.

claim: Polymerase backtracking and transcript termination were required to suppress hybrid-induced lethality.
source: By inference, polymerase backtracking and transcript termination were required to suppress hybrid-induced lethality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for Rpa12 and its known functions.

claim: The absence of the two RNases H leads to DNA damage that is difficult to repair after completion of S-phase.
source: Our observations in this study suggest that the absence of the two RNases H leads to DNA damage that is difficult to repair after completion of S-phase.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The increase in Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells begins at the exit from S-phase and continues until mid-M.
source: The increase in foci begins at the exit from S-phase and continues until mid-M.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DNA damage in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells induces a significant pre-anaphase delay by activating the Rad9-dependent checkpoint.
source: We show that this damage induces a significant pre-anaphase delay by activating the Rad9-dependent checkpoint.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When measured in a bulk population, Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells disappear slowly such that even after most cells have lost foci and completed cell division, a subset of cells retain foci and remain arrested pre-anaphase.
source: When measured in a bulk population, foci disappear slowly such that even after most cells have lost foci and completed cell division, a subset of cells retain foci and remain arrested pre-anaphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Disrupting factors that modulate BIR allows for repair of Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ TOP1-AID cells and restores cell division without reducing the initial level of damage.
source: Importantly, disrupting factors that modulate BIR allows for repair of these foci and restores cell division without reducing the initial level of damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The inability to repair damage, not the level of damage per se, in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells is the root cause of the inability to proceed through the cell cycle.
source: This demonstrates that the inability to repair damage, not the level of damage per se, in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells is the root cause of the inability to proceed through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that BIR inhibition allows repair without reducing initial damage levels.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids inhibit DNA repair.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DNA:RNA hybrids inhibit DNA repair and that a critical role of the RNases H is to remove hybrids so that efficient repair can occur.
evidence: This is a major conclusion inferred from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A critical role of the RNases H is to remove hybrids so that efficient repair can occur.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DNA:RNA hybrids inhibit DNA repair and that a critical role of the RNases H is to remove hybrids so that efficient repair can occur.
evidence: This is a major conclusion inferred from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inactivation of RNase H2 (rnh201∆) by itself leads to large increases of genomic hybrids and loss of heterozygosity compared to wild-type.
source: Inactivation of RNase H2 (rnh201∆) by itself leads to large increases of genomic hybrids and loss of heterozygosity compared to wild-type (Wahba et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wahba et al., 2016 and O'Connell et al., 2015.

claim: Dramatically elevated Rad52 foci are only observed in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells – not rnh201∆ cells.
source: However, dramatically elevated Rad52 foci are only observed in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells – not rnh201∆ cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Damage may be repaired rapidly in cells lacking RNase H2, while damage is repaired slowly in cells lacking both RNases H, causing foci to accumulate and persist.
source: We suggest that damage may be repaired rapidly in cells lacking RNase H2, while damage is repaired slowly in cells lacking both RNases H, causing foci to accumulate and persist.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the differential accumulation of foci in single versus double mutants.

claim: Inactivation of RNase H1 in sin3∆ cells increases genome instability further and skews the events from chromosome repair to chromosome loss.
source: Additionally, sin3∆ cells have elevated R-loops and hybrid-mediated genome instability. Inactivation of RNase H1 in sin3∆ cells increases genome instability further, but skews the events from chromosome repair to chromosome loss (Wahba et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wahba et al., 2011.

claim: The percent of repair by BIR was elevated about five fold in the rnh1∆ rnh201∆ double mutant compared to either of the singles or wild-type.
source: Furthermore, the percent of repair by BIR was elevated about five fold in the double mutant compared to either of the singles or wild-type, although validation of this difference awaits a larger sample size.
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connell et al., 2015 with a caveat about sample size.

claim: The RNases H remove hybrids from chromosomes both before and after R-loops induce DSBs.
source: To explain the BIR bias, we suggest that the RNases H remove hybrids from chromosomes both before and after R-loops induce DSBs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the absence of RNase H activity, more DSBs are induced and hybrids persist at these DSBs.
source: Conversely, in the absence of RNase H activity, more DSBs are induced and hybrids persist at these DSBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased damage in RNase H mutants.

claim: The presence of a hybrid on one free end of a DSB may block resection and/or invasion of homologous sequences, leading to failure to capture the second free end and resulting in BIR.
source: While one free end of the DSB may be properly processed by HR machinery, the presence of a hybrid on the opposite free end may block resection and/or invasion of homologous sequences. Ultimately, failure to capture the second free end of the DSB leads to BIR.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: The rDNA is the biggest source of R-loops in cells, accounting for almost 50% of all hybrids in yeast.
source: The rDNA is the biggest source of R-loops in cells, accounting for almost 50% of all hybrids in yeast (Wahba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wahba et al., 2016.

claim: Top1 inactivation preferentially induces genome instability in the rDNA.
source: In addition, Top1 inactivation preferentially induces genome instability in the rDNA (El Hage et al., 2010; Christman et al., 1993, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to El Hage et al., 2010; Christman et al., 1993, 1988.

claim: BIR at the rDNA may be particularly challenging in the presence of hybrids and even more challenging in the absence of Top1.
source: These results suggest that BIR at the rDNA may be particularly challenging in the presence of hybrids and even more challenging in the absence of Top1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing rDNA-specific lethality.

claim: The induction of hybrids in the rDNA generates a barrier to the processivity of DNA replication during BIR, thereby slowing repair.
source: We therefore propose that the induction of hybrids in the rDNA generates a barrier to the processivity of DNA replication during BIR, thereby slowing repair (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Further inactivation of Top1 causes elevated hybrids and stalled polymerases, which terminally block BIR replication fork progression.
source: Further inactivation of Top1 causes elevated hybrids and stalled polymerases, which we hypothesize terminally block BIR replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: The trapped BIR intermediate is an aberrant structure that leads to lethality.
source: This trapped BIR intermediate is an aberrant structure that then leads to lethality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing lethality in the triple mutant.

claim: The RPA190 suppressor mutations activate Rpa12, allowing it to remove stalled polymerases and possibly the associated hybrids, thereby removing the impediment to BIR imposed by Top1.
source: We therefore suggest that the RPA190 suppressor mutations activate Rpa12, allowing it to remove stalled polymerases and possibly the associated hybrids, thereby removing the impediment to BIR imposed by Top1 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and structural information, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: BIR is known to be a multi-step process in which strand invasion happens rapidly followed by a long delay before replication initiates.
source: Our model for stalled BIR intermediates as the cause of lethality in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ top1∆ cells is supported by the kinetics of repair and the molecular functions of Pif1 and Pol32. BIR is known to be a multi-step process in which strand invasion happens rapidly followed by a long delay before replication initiates (Jain et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jain et al., 2009.

claim: The long delay before replication initiates in BIR would explain the slow disappearance of hybrid-induced Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells.
source: This delay would explain the slow disappearance of hybrid-induced Rad52-GFP foci in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting known BIR kinetics to the observed slow foci disappearance.

claim: Pif1 and Pol32 are required for processivity of the BIR replication fork.
source: After this pause, Pif1 and Pol32 are required for processivity of the BIR replication fork.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of Pif1 and Pol32 causes the invading strand to dissociate before it can reach the blocks imposed by the hybrids and/or RNA polymerases.
source: We suggest that inhibition of these two factors causes the invading strand to dissociate before it can reach the blocks imposed by the hybrids and/or RNA polymerases.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: A slower, alternative pathway can repair the released strand after BIR is inhibited.
source: A slower, alternative pathway can then repair the released strand.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing repair occurs when BIR is inhibited.

claim: Single-strand annealing (SSA) may be involved in the alternative repair pathway.
source: The identity of this alternative repair pathway remains unclear, but we speculate that single-strand annealing (SSA) may be involved.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The high copy number of direct repeats present at the rDNA makes the locus an ideal substrate for SSA repair.
source: SSA is a form of HR that occurs when 5' to 3' resection uncovers complementary sequences that then anneal to each other, resulting in deletion of the intervening DNA. The high copy number of direct repeats present at the rDNA makes the locus an ideal substrate for this repair pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of SSA mechanism and rDNA structure.

claim: The kinetics of end resection (~4 kb/hr) and the size of a single rDNA repeat (9.1 kb) suggest that the repair of a DSB using SSA would take around 2–3 hr per repeat.
source: Additionally, the kinetics of end resection (~4 kb/hr) and the size of a single rDNA repeat (9.1 kb) suggest that the repair of a DSB using SSA would take around 2–3 hr per repeat (Fishman-Lobell et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an inference based on known resection kinetics from Fishman-Lobell et al., 1992 and rDNA repeat size.

claim: The estimated SSA repair time of 2–3 hr per repeat is consistent with the kinetics of Rad52-GFP foci dissolution observed in the study.
source: These estimates are consistent with the kinetics of Rad52-GFP foci dissolution seen here.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the calculated repair time to the observed data.

claim: The RNases H play a critical role in promoting proper repair of hybrid-induced DNA damage, particularly in highly transcribed repetitive DNA.
source: In summary, we show that the RNases H play a critical role in promoting proper repair of hybrid-induced DNA damage, particularly in highly transcribed repetitive DNA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many RNA biogenesis mutants induce hybrid formation and elevate genome instability.
source: For example, many RNA biogenesis mutants induce hybrid formation and elevate genome instability (Wahba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wahba et al., 2016.

claim: The genome instability of RNA biogenesis mutants can be suppressed by overexpression of RNase H.
source: The genome instability of these mutants can be suppressed by overexpression of RNase H, implying that RNase H activity becomes limiting when hybrid levels exceed a threshold.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Limiting RNase H activity in RNA biogenesis mutants likely allows hybrids to interfere with repair.
source: However, in light of our results, it is likely that limiting RNase H activity in these mutants also allows hybrids to interfere with repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of this study applied to other mutants.

claim: Many cancer cells contain highly transcribed amplicons.
source: Finally, the particular sensitivity of the highly transcribed rDNA repeats is intriguing given that many cancer cells contain highly transcribed amplicons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer cell biology.

claim: Highly transcribed amplicons in cancer cells may be not only sites of R-loop formation and R-loop induced DNA damage, but also sites of improper repair.
source: These amplicons may be not only sites of R-loop formation and R-loop induced DNA damage, but also sites of improper repair.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings for cancer biology.
